answer_sql:
SELECT
  COUNT(*) AS everyone_on_the_register_aged_25_to_44,
  COUNT(*) FILTER(WHERE
    was_a_customer_on_the_day) AS customers_on_that_day_aged_25_to_44,
  COUNT(*) FILTER(WHERE
    NOT was_a_customer_on_the_day) AS difference_had_already_left_the_register
FROM (
  SELECT
    (
      valid_from <= CAST('2022-12-10' AS DATE)
      AND valid_to >= CAST('2022-12-10' AS DATE)
    ) AS was_a_customer_on_the_day
  FROM contoso_served.dim_customer
  WHERE
    DATE_PART('year', AGE(CAST('2022-12-10' AS DATE), birth_date)) BETWEEN 25 AND 44
) AS t

body.value: The row I got back holds the two figures the question can mean and the distance between them, and it matches what I predicted before running it. Both numbers count PEOPLE, not orders or purchases: individuals on Contoso's customer register who had completed between 25 and 44 years of life on 10 December 2022, both ends of the band counted in, each person's age worked out from their own date of birth against that one day. 31,586 is all of them — everyone the register has ever held, out of 104,990 people, with the date used only to fix how old each one was. 24,787 is the narrower set whose register record was actually in force on that day. 6,799 is the first minus the second: people who were the right age on that date but whose customer record had closed before it. What neither figure includes: no filter on whether the person ever bought anything, none on country, gender, continent, state or channel, and no sales data in the count at all — the sales table was read once, separately, purely to test whether the record window carries meaning, and it contributed no row to either number.

value: Did you want everyone who has ever been on the customer register, or only the people who were actually customers on 10 December 2022? — (a) "Count everyone on the customer list, using their age as it was on that date": 31,586 customers. (b) "Count only people who were customers on that date, using their age on that date": 24,787 customers. The gap is 6,799 people who were aged 25-44 on that day but whose register record had already closed before it. I tried to settle this and could not: the record window looked at first like bookkeeping noise, but across all 223,974 sales not one purchase was ever made after a buyer's record closed, and the last order from any of those 6,799 was 25 November 2022 — so the window behaves like a genuine membership period, which makes (b) a serious reading. Against that, the ontology defines a Customer as the register of 104,990 people and declares nothing about reading that register as of a date, which makes (a) a serious reading. Tell me which and I will hand you the single number. WHAT YOUR CHOICE DOES NOT CHANGE: reading the date as 12 October 2022 instead of 10 December moves (a) by 2 people and (b) by 98, so the day.month ordering genuinely does not matter here; counting age by birth year instead of completed years moves (a) by 24 and (b) by 20; and reading "between 25 and 44" as excluding its ends gives 28,328 and 22,202 — lower on both, but it does not decide between them.

Both figures were computed over contoso_served.dim_customer restricted to the 31,586 people who had completed 25 to 44 years of life on 10 December 2022 — that age band applied to the full 104,990-row register established at step 1, with no other restriction of any kind. Within that band, 31,586 is every one of them and 24,787 is the subset whose `valid_from`/`valid_to` window covers 10 December 2022; that window is the only difference between the two numbers. I applied no purchase filter, no country, gender, continent or channel filter, and no join to sales — the sales table was queried once, separately, only to test whether the validity window carries meaning, and it contributed no row to either figure.

value.means: One row holding the two populations this step can mean, both taken from the 104,990-person register that step 1 settled, both pinned to the single day 10 December 2022. The first is everybody on the register — 104,990 — because the date is read as nothing but the moment at which to compute ages. The second is only those whose customer record was in force on that day. The remaining columns say where the gap comes from: how many records had already closed before that day, and how many had not yet begun (none, since every registration predates 2011). No age band is applied here; that is the next step. What this step establishes is that the two readings are not the same set of people and the difference is not small.

readings.could_also_mean: 12 October 2022, month.day.year — and I measured it rather than guessing: the 25-to-44 count is 31,586 on 10 December against 31,588 on 12 October over the whole register, and 24,787 against 24,885 over customers in force. Two people and ninety-eight people respectively, on counts above twenty-four thousand. This fork is immaterial either way, so I have taken the European reading and will not spend a question on it.

SELECT
  COUNT(*) AS pop_whole_register,
  COUNT(*) FILTER(WHERE
    in_force) AS pop_customers_on_the_day,
  COUNT(*) FILTER(WHERE
    completed_age BETWEEN 25 AND 44) AS register_completed_inclusive,
  COUNT(*) FILTER(WHERE
    in_force AND completed_age BETWEEN 25 AND 44) AS onday_completed_inclusive,
  COUNT(*) FILTER(WHERE
    completed_age BETWEEN 26 AND 43) AS register_completed_exclusive,
  COUNT(*) FILTER(WHERE
    in_force AND completed_age BETWEEN 26 AND 43) AS onday_completed_exclusive,
  COUNT(*) FILTER(WHERE
    calendar_age BETWEEN 25 AND 44) AS register_calendaryear_inclusive,
  COUNT(*) FILTER(WHERE
    in_force AND calendar_age BETWEEN 25 AND 44) AS onday_calendaryear_inclusive,
  COUNT(*) FILTER(WHERE
    completed_age = 25) AS register_exactly_25,
  COUNT(*) FILTER(WHERE
    completed_age = 44) AS register_exactly_44
FROM (
  SELECT
    (
      valid_from <= CAST('2022-12-10' AS DATE)
      AND valid_to >= CAST('2022-12-10' AS DATE)
    ) AS in_force,
    DATE_PART('year', AGE(CAST('2022-12-10' AS DATE), birth_date)) AS completed_age,
    2022 - DATE_PART('year', birth_date) AS calendar_age
  FROM contoso_served.dim_customer
) AS t

SELECT
  COUNT(*) AS everyone_on_the_register_aged_25_to_44,
  COUNT(*) FILTER(WHERE
    was_a_customer_on_the_day) AS customers_on_that_day_aged_25_to_44,
  COUNT(*) FILTER(WHERE
    NOT was_a_customer_on_the_day) AS difference_had_already_left_the_register
FROM (
  SELECT
    (
      valid_from <= CAST('2022-12-10' AS DATE)
      AND valid_to >= CAST('2022-12-10' AS DATE)
    ) AS was_a_customer_on_the_day
  FROM contoso_served.dim_customer
  WHERE
    DATE_PART('year', AGE(CAST('2022-12-10' AS DATE), birth_date)) BETWEEN 25 AND 44
) AS t
